newsitem.title: ITALY: Employers tell Italy govt to stay out of metal row.
newsitem.headline: Employers tell Italy govt to stay out of metal row.

text.p: The Italian government should not intervene in the current pay dispute in the metal industry, Giorgio Fossa, the leader of employers' federation Confindustria, told reporters on Friday.

Some 1.5 million engineering and metalworkers announced on Thursday a fresh round of strikes to press their pay claim while union leaders will decide later this month whether to widen the conflict to include other industrial sectors.

Negotiations between management and workers over the renewal of contracts for the 1997-98 period broke down last month and no fresh talks are scheduled. Industry Minister Pierluigi Bersani on Thursday would not rule out government intervention.
When asked if he would welcome the government around the negotiating table, Fossa replied: "Absolutely not."
At the heart of the dispute lies a labour deal signed in July 1993 by unions, employers and the government.
Under the terms of the pact, automatic index-linking of salaries was abolished, but management undertook to make up any shortfall in wages if inflation ran above government targets.

However the wording of the accord was deliberately vague. Unions have interpreted it to mean that all the inflation overshoot should be covered, employers argue that only a part of lost earnings need be made up. The government has kept silent.
"The government still hasn't explained what it thinks of the 1993 accord. Once they've done that then they can join the negotiating table," Fossa said on Friday. -- Crispian Balmer +396 6782501
